paragraphs: This paper speeds up training for regression trees whose leaves contain linear predictors. It starts from Tree Alternating Optimization, or TAO, which repeatedly improves a tree rather than constructing it through greedy splits. The abstract describes TAO as guaranteeing a decreasing training objective and producing smaller, more accurate trees than traditional greedy approaches.

The proposed modification preserves TAO’s result while changing how each leaf’s predictor is optimized. At any iteration, a leaf receives only part of the training data. The Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury formula lets the algorithm exploit that smaller subset to solve the same optimization problem more efficiently, with particular benefits for high-dimensional inputs or deep trees.

The complexity analysis yields a surprising conditional result: beyond a critical depth, a larger tree can train faster because individual leaf problems become smaller. This can even make tree training asymptotically faster than ordinary linear regression. Experiments verify speedups across datasets. The reasoning also applies to other trees when node optimization costs grow faster than linearly with the number of assigned examples.
neurips-2025-a-faster-training-algorithm.tldr: An exact reformulation accelerates TAO training and explains why sufficiently deep regression trees can become faster to train as they grow.

paragraphs: Virtual screening seeks promising drug candidates using protein structures, but many methods assume that the binding pocket is already known from a protein bound to a ligand. Early discovery often has only unbound or predicted structures. AANet addresses this mismatch by learning to screen candidates when the location and structure of the binding site are uncertain.

The framework combines alignment with aggregation. A contrastive learning component brings together representations of ligands, known bound pockets, and cavities detected in protein structures. This aims to make predictions less sensitive to pocket localization errors. A cross-attention adapter then combines information from candidate binding sites, allowing learning from activity measurements without precise pocket annotations.

On a newly assembled benchmark of unbound structures, AANet improves the reported early enrichment factor at 1% from 11.75 to 37.19 in the blind screening setting. It also retains strong performance on bound structures. These findings support the approach’s promise for discovery settings without experimentally resolved protein-ligand complexes, where uncertainty about the pocket is part of the screening problem.
neurips-2025-aanet-virtual-screening-und.tldr: AANet aligns molecular and pocket representations and combines candidate binding sites to improve virtual screening under structural uncertainty.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization tries to find good solutions with a limited number of evaluations. Its Gaussian process model depends heavily on a kernel, which shapes how observations inform predictions about unexplored candidates. A poorly matched kernel can slow progress or lead to weaker solutions. This paper makes kernel design adaptive throughout the optimization process.

The method, Context-Aware Kernel Evolution, or CAKE, uses a language model to generate and refine kernels from the observations collected so far. The language model acts as the crossover and mutation operators in this evolutionary process. Kernel candidates can therefore change as additional evaluations reveal more about the objective being optimized.

A companion ranking procedure, BAKER, balances model fit measured by the Bayesian information criterion with expected improvement. This connects kernel selection to both explaining existing observations and guiding the next optimization step. Experiments report consistent improvements over established baselines across hyperparameter optimization, controller tuning, and photonic chip design. The findings support adapting the model’s kernel as part of optimization rather than relying throughout on an initially selected kernel.
neurips-2025-adaptive-kernel-design-for-.tldr: CAKE uses language models to evolve Gaussian process kernels during Bayesian optimization and ranks them by fit and expected improvement.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify the main directions of variation while protecting each individual input through differential privacy. Its inputs are independent, identically distributed random matrices with a shared expectation. The goal is to estimate a subspace of dimension k that captures the largest-variance directions of that expectation.

Existing approaches face two problems highlighted in the abstract: they may need sample counts growing faster than the dimension, or add excessive privacy noise when the inputs themselves have little randomness. Earlier work addressed both issues for a single leading direction. The proposed iterative algorithm extends this capability to any number of leading directions up to the full dimension.

For one direction, the method matches the earlier algorithm’s utility guarantees and obtains nearly optimal statistical error with sample size approximately linear in dimension, up to logarithmic factors. For multiple directions, the authors give a lower bound within a factor of k of their upper bound. Experiments also show advantages over comparable baselines, complementing the theoretical account of privacy and estimation accuracy.
neurips-2025-an-iterative-algorithm-for-.tldr: An adaptive-noise private PCA algorithm estimates multiple leading directions while addressing excessive noise and unfavorable sample requirements.

paragraphs: CAGE reconstructs vector floorplans from density maps derived from point clouds. Noisy or incomplete observations can make corner-based representations produce broken or implausible room layouts. Methods that group lines use more structural information, but the abstract identifies remaining difficulty in recovering fine geometric details.

The proposed representation treats each wall segment as a directed edge with geometric continuity. This puts connected wall geometry at the center of reconstruction, supporting closed, topologically valid room boundaries while reducing artifacts. A transformer decoder combines perturbed queries with latent queries in a denoising framework. The authors report that this design stabilizes optimization and speeds convergence.

Experiments on Structured3D and SceneCAD report state-of-the-art performance, with F1 scores of 99.1% for rooms, 91.7% for corners, and 89.3% for angles. The method also shows strong generalization across datasets. Together, these results support the value of representing walls as continuous edges: the same formulation addresses coherent room structure and the finer geometric details needed for a useful floorplan.
neurips-2025-cage-continuity-aware-edge-.tldr: CAGE models walls as continuous directed edges to reconstruct coherent, detailed floorplans from point-cloud density maps.

paragraphs: This paper examines arguments about whether AI should be democratized. It separates two unresolved questions: what democratizing AI actually means, and whether pursuing it is ethically and politically desirable. These disagreements concern both the definition of the goal and the reasons society might have for supporting or rejecting it.

The authors identify eight recurring traps in skeptical arguments about AI democratization. They characterize these as objections that initially appear convincing but rest on misconceptions, and develop responses to each. The contribution is therefore an analysis of the reasoning used in the debate, helping distinguish objections that deserve weight from arguments the authors consider misleading.

Their conclusion remains qualified: democratization may have drawbacks, but it should not be dismissed prematurely on mistaken grounds. The paper also offers a constructive roadmap for alternative ways to define and evaluate democratizing AI while avoiding the identified traps. Its practical significance is to keep conceptual disagreement and ethical judgment explicit, so that rejecting an argument against democratization does not automatically settle which form of democratization should be pursued.
neurips-2025-dont-give-up-on-democratizi.tldr: The paper challenges eight misconceptions in arguments against democratizing AI while acknowledging that democratization may still have drawbacks.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why language models still make balanced-parentheses errors despite their broader coding abilities. Studying models ranging from 124 million to 7 billion parameters, the authors examine how internal components contribute to token predictions. Their explanation focuses on competition among mechanisms already present inside the models.

Some attention heads and feed-forward neurons reliably favor correct answers across a range of inputs. Others are less dependable and promote incorrect tokens. In the studied errors, these faulty contributions outweigh the reliable ones. This means an incorrect output can arise even when useful internal mechanisms are available but do not exert enough influence on the final prediction.

The authors introduce RASteer to identify reliable components and increase their contribution. On balanced-parentheses tasks, it raises some models’ accuracy from 0% to around 100%, without impairing general coding ability in the reported evaluation. Arithmetic reasoning experiments show gains of up to around 20%. These findings support targeted steering as a way to improve performance by changing the balance between existing internal mechanisms.
neurips-2025-failure-by-interference-lan.tldr: RASteer improves syntactic and arithmetic performance by strengthening reliable model components that can otherwise be overshadowed by faulty ones.

paragraphs: Human intervention can guide an agent while it learns, but the resulting data mix human and agent behavior. That mixture changes as the agent develops, and delayed interventions introduce further imperfections. FaithDaIL addresses the challenge of using these data efficiently while remaining faithful to the human expert’s policy.

The authors formulate learning as an online, non-convex optimization problem. Dynamic regret minimization helps the learner adapt to changing trajectory distributions and track high-quality policy trajectories. This explicitly accounts for the evolving behavior that generates training data, rather than treating the learning setting as fixed throughout training.

A second component introduces an unbiased imitation objective. It uses weighting based on the behavior distribution relative to the human expert’s distribution as a proxy reward, addressing the mixed origin of the examples. On the MetaDrive and CARLA driving benchmarks, FaithDaIL reports state-of-the-art safety and task success while requiring substantially less human intervention data than prior human-in-the-loop baselines. The results connect distribution-aware learning with more efficient use of expert supervision.
neurips-2025-faithful-dynamic-imitation-.tldr: FaithDaIL combines dynamic regret minimization with an unbiased imitation objective to learn effectively from changing mixtures of agent and human behavior.

paragraphs: Lens flare reduces image quality when cameras face strong light sources. Training a removal model requires corresponding images with and without flare, but capturing such pairs in real scenes is difficult. Existing datasets often overlay artificial flare templates on images, with limited template variety and insufficient attention to physical illumination.

FlareX addresses these weaknesses through a three-stage data-generation process. It creates parameterized flare templates, synthesizes two-dimensional examples with illumination-aware rules, and uses a physical engine to render three-dimensional scenes. Combining these sources gives the dataset both varied image-plane flare patterns and examples generated within a modeled scene.

The dataset contains 9,500 two-dimensional templates derived from 95 patterns, along with 3,000 rendered image pairs from 60 three-dimensional scenes. The authors also develop a masking approach for obtaining flare-free real-world images from corrupted counterparts, supporting evaluation on real imagery. Their experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the generation method and dataset. The contribution links the realism and diversity of training examples to the challenge of making flare removal work outside synthetic data.
neurips-2025-flarex-a-physics-informed-d.tldr: FlareX combines illumination-aware 2D synthesis and physical 3D rendering to create more varied, physically informed training data for lens-flare removal.

paragraphs: This paper predicts where a person’s visual attention will focus next in their three-dimensional surroundings. It extends egocentric understanding beyond motion and physical interaction to forecasting visual perception itself. The task is relevant to systems such as augmented reality, virtual reality, and assistive technologies that could benefit from anticipating what a user will look at.

EgoSpanLift moves visual-span forecasting from two-dimensional images into three-dimensional scenes. It converts keypoints obtained through simultaneous localization and mapping into geometry compatible with gaze, then extracts volumetric regions representing visual span. A 3D U-Net and unidirectional transformers combine spatial structure with temporal information to predict future regions in a three-dimensional grid.

The authors also build a benchmark containing 364.6 thousand samples from raw egocentric multisensory data. Their method outperforms competitive baselines for gaze anticipation and three-dimensional localization. When its predictions are projected back onto image planes, it achieves comparable results without additional training specific to two-dimensional prediction. This suggests that the three-dimensional formulation can support scene-level forecasting while retaining usefulness for image-based evaluation.
neurips-2025-gaze-beyond-the-frame-forec.tldr: EgoSpanLift forecasts future visual attention in 3D by combining gaze-compatible scene geometry with spatial and temporal modeling.

paragraphs: Target sound extraction isolates selected sounds from a mixture using a clue about what to retain. A teacher model can receive extra information about the target during training and transfer what it learns to a student. However, overly rich information can make the teacher overfit and leave the student unable to benefit effectively.

Disentangled Codec Knowledge Distillation regulates both the amount of extra information and where it enters the teacher. A neural audio codec compresses the target sound. Disentangled representation learning then removes class information from that representation while retaining fine temporal information. Separately, an n-hot vector supplies the target’s class information.

Class information conditions early teacher layers, while the class-independent temporal representation conditions later layers, creating a coarse-to-fine flow of information. Feature-level distillation transfers the resulting representation to the student, which does not require the privileged information at use time. Experiments report consistent improvements across existing methods and model architectures under multi-target selection. The findings support organizing privileged knowledge carefully, rather than simply providing the teacher with a richer target description.
neurips-2025-improving-target-sound-extr.tldr: DCKD improves sound extraction by compressing and separating privileged target information before transferring teacher features to a student.

paragraphs: LeMiCa accelerates diffusion-based video generation without additional training. It addresses a problem in caching strategies that reduce computation: locally reasonable reuse decisions can accumulate errors across generation. The resulting video may drift in content or style from the output of the original, unaccelerated process.

The authors represent cache scheduling as a directed graph whose edges carry error weights. They then use lexicographic minimax path optimization to explicitly bound the worst-case path error. This makes the accumulated consequences of a schedule central to the decision, supporting greater consistency of content and style across the generated frames.

Experiments on multiple text-to-video benchmarks report improvements in speed and generation quality over prior caching techniques. Specific results include a 2.9-fold speedup on Latte and an LPIPS score of 0.05 on Open-Sora. The abstract reports minimal perceptual degradation from the acceleration. These findings support treating caching as a global scheduling problem, because the quality of a sequence depends on how errors combine across the generation process.
neurips-2025-lemica-lexicographic-minima.tldr: LeMiCa accelerates diffusion video generation by optimizing cache schedules around accumulated worst-case error.

paragraphs: Information diffusion prediction forecasts which users will be reached next as information spreads through a social platform. Existing graph and sequence models emphasize network connections and timing. The paper argues that these signals can leave models with misleading diffusion links and insufficient context for explaining how information actually spreads.

MILD uses a language model within a causal framework to infer diffusion influence links. It combines four sources of evidence: social connections, activity timelines, user profiles, and comments. The inferred links form a dedicated influence graph, intended to represent the spreading process more faithfully than the underlying social network alone.

The authors introduce evaluation measures for assessing this graph’s quality and reliability in diffusion prediction. They report an absolute improvement of 12% over social network structure in their structural evaluation, alongside state-of-the-art prediction performance. The abstract does not identify that improvement as a specific familiar accuracy metric. Its stated implication is that richer contextual inference can produce a more useful diffusion structure, with potential benefits for explainable and trustworthy public opinion analysis.
neurips-2025-make-information-diffusion-.tldr: MILD combines social connections, timing, profiles, and comments to infer an influence graph that improves information diffusion prediction.

paragraphs: Metric Automata Theory extends classical automata theory to continuous dynamical systems, providing a common framework for recurrent neural networks, including xLSTM and state space models. It handles both finite and unbounded numerical precision. Its notion of robustness guarantees numerical stability and contributes to learning stability.

The theory distinguishes what these architectures can represent robustly. The authors show that xLSTM can robustly model all star-free regular languages, whereas state space models cannot robustly recognize the FLIP-FLOP language. This offers a theoretical perspective on the importance of nonlinear recurrence and insight into xLSTM’s stronger performance on several tasks.

The analysis also clarifies Mamba’s capabilities. Under finite precision, Mamba cannot generally recognize star-free languages, but its state space can be separated in a piecewise-linear way that supports approximations with some generalization to longer sequences. The authors show that this state-space structure is unavailable for languages such as Parity. This distinction reconciles limitations on exact recognition with reported empirical success on star-free languages and failure on Parity.
neurips-2025-metric-automata-theory-a-un.tldr: Metric Automata Theory explains how robustness and numerical precision shape the sequence-recognition capabilities of recurrent architectures.

paragraphs: Machine learning interatomic potentials support molecular and materials modeling, but evaluating them presents problems beyond measuring prediction error. The abstract identifies data leakage, limited transferability, and heavy dependence on particular density functional theory references as weaknesses of existing benchmarks. MLIP Arena broadens the evaluation to behaviors that matter in physical applications.

The platform assesses awareness of physical principles, chemical reactivity, stability under extreme conditions, and prediction of thermodynamic properties and physical phenomena. These dimensions examine how a force field behaves across different scientific demands. They complement comparisons against static reference calculations by making physical consistency and behavior part of the assessment.

The authors report that this approach exposes important failure modes of current foundation interatomic potentials in real-world settings. They provide a reproducible framework, a Python package, and an online leaderboard to support transparent comparison. The intended role is to guide future models toward better predictive accuracy and runtime efficiency while preserving physical consistency. The contribution is an evaluation platform that makes these objectives visible together when assessing progress.
neurips-2025-mlip-arena-advancing-fairne.tldr: MLIP Arena evaluates interatomic potentials through physical behavior, reactivity, stability, and thermodynamic prediction alongside broader development goals.

paragraphs: DiPro models disease progression using sequences of chest X-rays together with electronic health records. Combining these sources is difficult because successive images contain much unchanged anatomy, while clinically relevant changes may be less prominent. Imaging also arrives sparsely and irregularly, creating timing mismatches with the more continuous health-record data.

The framework first separates static anatomical features from dynamic features associated with pathology progression. This region-aware separation prioritizes changes relevant to disease over repeated visual content. It then aligns both types of imaging features with asynchronous health records at two timescales: local intervals and the full sequence.

The two alignment levels connect nearby observations while also modeling a coherent progression across the complete record. Experiments on MIMIC indicate that DiPro can extract temporal clinical dynamics and achieve state-of-the-art performance on disease progression identification and general intensive-care prediction tasks. These findings support jointly addressing visual redundancy and temporal mismatch when learning from longitudinal multimodal data. The reported contribution concerns modeling and prediction on those tasks, rather than a demonstrated change in clinical care.
neurips-2025-multimodal-disease-progress.tldr: DiPro separates anatomical stability from disease-related changes and aligns X-rays with health records across local and global timescales.

paragraphs: OmniTry extends virtual try-on beyond clothing to wearable objects such as jewelry and accessories. It also removes the need for an explicit placement mask. A central difficulty is collecting paired examples that show both a particular object and its corresponding appearance when worn, especially across varied object categories.

The framework uses two training stages. First, it learns placement from large collections of unpaired portraits containing wearable items. An inpainting model is repurposed to draw objects in appropriate positions when given an empty mask. Second, paired images refine its ability to preserve the appearance of the specific object being transferred.

The authors observe that the first stage enables rapid convergence during paired training, even with few paired examples. Evaluation covers 12 common wearable categories using both shop imagery and images captured in everyday settings. Results suggest better object localization and identity preservation than existing methods. The approach therefore separates learning where wearable objects belong from learning to reproduce their particular appearance, addressing two requirements of broader, mask-free virtual try-on.
neurips-2025-omnitry-virtual-try-on-anyt.tldr: OmniTry learns mask-free placement from unpaired portraits, then uses paired examples to preserve the appearance of diverse wearable objects.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes the convergence of AdamW, an optimizer widely used for training large language models. It measures progress through the gradient’s ℓ1 norm, which adds the absolute values of its coordinates. The result bounds the expected gradient norm averaged across K iterations, providing a theoretical description of how this quantity decreases.

The bound scales as O(√d C/K^(1/4)), where d is the model dimension and C matches the constant in SGD’s optimal convergence rate. Interpreting the dimension factor requires attention to the norm being measured. The authors therefore compare the ℓ1 measure with the ℓ2 gradient norm used in their discussion of SGD.

When each gradient coordinate follows a standard Gaussian distribution, they establish a relationship in expectation involving a factor proportional to √d. Their deep-learning experiments also observe ℓ1 gradient norms scaling as √d times the ℓ2 norm. The conditional theoretical relationship and empirical observations support viewing AdamW’s bound as analogous to SGD’s optimal rate. They do not establish an unconditional equality between the norms for every gradient.
neurips-2025-on-the-o-frac-sqrt-d-k-1-4-.tldr: The paper proves an ℓ1-gradient convergence bound for AdamW and gives theoretical and empirical support for comparing it with SGD’s optimal rate.

paragraphs: PC-Net locates video moments described by language while training only on video-query pairs, without exact temporal annotations. The paper introduces weakly supervised compositional moment retrieval, emphasizing generalization to queries with unfamiliar vocabulary combinations or syntactic structures. This demands more than recognizing language patterns already encountered during training.

Frozen feature extractors first represent the video and query, and cross-modal interaction combines their information. A dual-granularity generator uses global and frame-level features to propose relevant time intervals. Within each proposal, semantic alignment and a learnable peak-aware Gaussian weighting mechanism combine frame features into a representation of the candidate moment.

Proposal quality is assessed by how well its features reconstruct a masked query. A further regularizer separates proposals by query relevance and uses contrastive learning to strengthen meaningful associations while suppressing spurious correlations. Experiments on Charades-CG and ActivityNet-CG demonstrate generalization across diverse compositional queries. The method reports superior performance with 54% fewer parameters than prior work, linking its proposal-centered design to both retrieval quality and parameter efficiency.
neurips-2025-pc-net-weakly-supervised-co.tldr: PC-Net learns to retrieve moments for compositional video queries without timestamp labels by generating, representing, and evaluating query-relevant proposals.

paragraphs: Retrosynthesis plans how to build a target molecule by working backward toward available starting materials. The plan forms a tree, and every terminal branch must reach a valid building block. A single unresolved branch invalidates the whole route, making average performance across branches an incomplete guide to planning quality.

The authors formulate this weakest-link problem as worst-path optimization in a tree-structured Markov decision process. They prove that the formulation has a unique optimal solution and supports monotonic improvement. InterRetro builds on this result by learning a value function for worst-path outcomes and using self-imitation to reinforce past decisions with high estimated advantage.

In the reported experiments, InterRetro solves all targets in the Retro*-190 benchmark and shortens synthetic routes by 4.9%. It also achieves promising results using only 10% of the training data. These findings support aligning the learning objective with the branch that can cause an entire plan to fail. The complete success result applies to the named benchmark, while the theoretical guarantees concern the proposed optimization formulation.
neurips-2025-retrosynthesis-planning-via.tldr: InterRetro improves retrosynthesis planning by optimizing the weakest branch of a synthesis tree and reinforcing successful past decisions.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction constructs prediction bands with finite-sample coverage, but making those bands adapt well to individual test cases remains challenging. This paper builds on an approach that treats band construction as a statistical learning problem directly targeting coverage and adaptivity. The formulation uses kernel Hilbert spaces and kernel sum-of-squares methods.

The authors extend the theory with a general representer theorem and derive a dual optimization problem. This dual can be solved using accelerated gradient methods with hundreds or thousands of samples. That provides a computational alternative to earlier approaches relying on general-purpose semidefinite programming solvers.

They also introduce a hyperparameter selection strategy based on the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion, using bounds on test-conditional coverage to target adaptivity. In their framework, the strategy tunes kernel lengthscales. The authors suggest that it could also apply to other conformal methods with learned score functions. Experiments compare the method with related work. The contribution combines more efficient optimization with a tuning objective explicitly concerned with how coverage behaves for test cases.
neurips-2025-scalable-and-adaptive-predi.tldr: A kernel sum-of-squares approach makes prediction-band learning more scalable and introduces coverage-focused tuning for adaptivity.

paragraphs: This paper explores neural networks that can change their structure during training. Its motivation comes from biological plasticity and from the dependence of many artificial networks on carefully designed, often oversized architectures. The aim is to develop networks that remain capable while using a more streamlined and adaptable structure.

The authors first introduce the Graph Perceptron as an extension of the multilayer perceptron. They then add a self-assembly mechanism to create the Self-Assembling Graph Perceptron, or SAGP. During training, SAGP can adjust how many neurons and connections it contains, as well as how those components connect to one another.

The reported results show comparable or better performance using about 5% of the size of an MLP. The authors also demonstrate advantages for interpretability and feature selection. These findings support learning aspects of network structure alongside the training process, allowing model size and connectivity to adapt. The size comparison concerns the MLP comparison reported in the study; its significance is that substantial structural reduction can coexist with strong performance in those evaluations.
neurips-2025-self-assembling-graph-perce.tldr: SAGP adapts its neurons and connections during training, achieving comparable or better performance at about 5% of an MLP’s size.

paragraphs: Spectral mean flows approach sequence modeling through representations of probability distributions. Operator theory describes nonlinear probabilistic dynamics using linear maps in a suitable Hilbert space. Building on this perspective for hidden Markov models, the paper embeds an entire sequence distribution as a tensor instead of explicitly constructing stochastic recurrence.

Generation is formulated as a maximum mean discrepancy gradient flow over sequences. Two computational problems then arise: the distribution tensors can become large, and sampling can converge slowly. The proposed algorithm addresses the first through spectral decomposition of linear operators, producing a scalable tensor-network representation of sequence mean embeddings.

For the second problem, the authors extend these gradient flows to time-dependent Hilbert spaces and connect them to flow matching through the continuity equation. This enables simulation-free learning and faster sampling. Experiments report competitive results across time-series modeling datasets. The contribution connects a distribution-level view of sequence dynamics with a tractable neural architecture and a more efficient generative procedure, making the operator-theoretic formulation usable for sequence modeling.
neurips-2025-sequence-modeling-with-spec.tldr: Spectral mean flows combine operator-based sequence representations, tensor networks, and flow matching for tractable time-series generation.

paragraphs: StreamBridge adapts video language models designed for offline inputs to ongoing video streams. The paper identifies two challenges: maintaining understanding across real-time conversational turns and responding proactively. Addressing both is necessary for an assistant that follows unfolding video while continuing an interaction.

The framework adds a memory buffer with round-decayed compression to support long-context, multi-turn use. It also introduces a separate lightweight activation model that enables proactive responses and can be integrated with existing video language models. These components address retaining useful interaction context and activating responses during continuous input.

The authors additionally create Stream-IT, a large streaming-video instruction dataset with interleaved video and text and varied instruction formats. Experiments report substantial improvements in streaming understanding across tasks, including results exceeding GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro in the evaluated settings. StreamBridge also achieves competitive or stronger results on standard video understanding benchmarks. Together, the findings support extending existing offline models through memory, response activation, and streaming-oriented training data while retaining strong conventional video understanding.
neurips-2025-streambridge-turning-your-o.tldr: StreamBridge adds compressed memory and a lightweight activation model to make offline video language models support proactive streaming interactions.

paragraphs: This paper brings convolution-like inductive biases into vision transformers through initialization. Convolutional networks have built-in structure that supports learning from smaller datasets. The authors aim to give transformers similar benefits at the start of training while preserving their ability to perform well as more data become available.

The approach is motivated by an empirical observation that random impulse filters can perform comparably to learned filters within a convolutional network. Rather than changing the transformer architecture, the method gives its initial weights useful structure. This differs from initialization strategies that focus on weight distributions or borrow attention weights from pretrained models without explicitly enforcing such structure.

Experiments report substantial improvements over standard vision-transformer initialization on small and medium-scale benchmarks, including Food-101, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, STL-10, Flowers, and Pets. Performance remains comparable on ImageNet-1K. The strategy also produces consistent improvements when integrated into Swin Transformer and MLP-Mixer. These results support initialization as a practical place to introduce helpful prior structure while allowing subsequent training to develop the model.
neurips-2025-structured-initialization-f.tldr: Structured initialization gives vision transformers convolution-like learning biases, improving smaller-data performance while retaining comparable large-scale results.
